messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 78
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event
  Memory: Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Vignette:
Elena Weber is a 78-year-old graphic designer who came to treatment after years of trying to keep one part of her life sealed off from the rest. She is a white American woman of European family background, married, and still works, mostly from home now, on freelance design projects for local businesses and nonprofit newsletters. She speaks clearly and precisely about color, layout, and proportion, but when she turns to the disaster that divided her life into before and after, her account shifts in striking ways: at times flat and detached, at other times as immediate as if the room around her has fallen away.

The event occurred during a severe natural disaster that struck her community with little protection and left multiple families devastated. Elena remembers being at home and then, in fragments, the chaos of the house no longer feeling solid or safe, doors banging violently in the force of the storm, and the sickly sharp smell of alcohol afterward as emergency responders and displaced neighbors moved through damaged buildings with disinfectants, spilled drinks, and the odor clinging to people who had been shocked, sleepless, or drinking to get through the night. She recalls hearing, in the aftermath, who had not made it, who was still missing, which family had lost a spouse, which household had lost a child. Those reports lodged in her mind with a particular force. Even now, when people talk about others losing loved ones, she feels herself pulled back toward that time. What she says most often is not only that it was terrifying, but that it should not have happened the way it did. In her mind there were failures, preventable failures, and the fact that nothing meaningful was ever put right has remained a live injury.

In the months that followed, Elena tried to carry on. She returned to design work, opening files, adjusting fonts, sending drafts to clients, trying to reenter the orderly world of margins and grids. But ordinary moments in that world became charged. If a delivery door slammed in the hallway of her studio building, her body reacted before she could think; for a moment the memory was not memory at all, but the event itself, happening now. A client pushing open the conference room door too fast could leave her frozen, heart racing, disoriented by the certainty that danger had come back. The smell of alcohol could do something similar. If she met a client in a restaurant and a server passed carrying wine, or if she caught the stale odor of liquor on someone’s breath, she would lose track of the present. At other times she could recount pieces of the disaster in a voice so calm and bloodless that even she felt disturbed by it, as if she were describing a scene from someone else’s life. She has said more than once that the story feels unreal to her, too extreme to belong to her own biography.

Elena developed small, rigid habits that made sense to her because they offered a feeling of control she no longer trusted the world to provide. She began cleaning and reorganizing her home office repeatedly, straightening stacks of sample paper, wiping surfaces, aligning pens and rulers, emptying drawers and arranging them again. If she felt unsettled after hearing a door bang in the apartment building, she might spend an hour scrubbing the kitchen counters or alphabetizing supply cabinets. She also found herself dwelling over and over on how the disaster could have been prevented—what officials should have done, what warnings should have been issued differently, what structures should have been reinforced, what decisions might have spared families from loss. These thoughts did not feel optional to her; they felt like the only honest response to something so unfair. Alongside that, she made determined efforts not to think about the event at all. She would cut off conversations, turn away from news coverage, and mentally push images aside, trying to erase them before they took hold.

Over time, these patterns narrowed her life. She became wary of stories about bereavement and avoided community gatherings where disaster anniversaries might be mentioned. Her husband noticed that she would abruptly leave the room if a television segment turned to families mourning loved ones. Work also changed. Elena started declining in-person meetings when possible, preferring the predictability of remote contact. She remained capable and exacting in her design work, but more of her day was spent trying to keep herself steady enough to do it.

What she says has been most damaged is her basic sense of how the world works. She had once believed that if people were responsible and institutions did their jobs, there was some order to things. Now she is certain the world is dangerous, that safety is fragile and easily stripped away, and that terrible losses can descend without remedy. The final push to seek help came recently, when a client meeting in an office corridor was interrupted by a heavy door slamming behind someone. Elena felt instantly transported back, then spent the evening cleaning her apartment in silence while her husband watched, worried and shut out. She came in saying she is tired of living as if the disaster is still waiting behind the next sound, and afraid that if she does not find some way to face what happened, the rest of her life will continue to shrink around it.
